newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU under pressure to increase justice role.
newsitem.headline: EU under pressure to increase justice role.

text.p: European Union justice ministers on Thursday stepped up pressure to boost the bloc's role in fighting crime after reviewing evidence that three years of limited cooperation between member states has had little effect.

France, traditionally wary of ceding sovereignty over justice matters, confirmed a recent tendency to side with Germany in its bid for a legal dimension for what started as an economic and trade bloc.

"Over the next five years we should progressively reach a common space of free movement for people and goods, but at the same time security should be increased," French Justice Minister Alain Toubon told a news conference after the second day of an informal Justice and Home Affairs Council.
The future of cooperation in this area is one of the most difficult aspects of talks in the EU's current intergovernmental conference drafting a new EU treaty.

Toubon was quoted by diplomats as telling the meeting that cooperation should be stepped up in the fight against drugs and terrorism, and proposing that the EU could take over responsibility for immigration and asylum matters if institutional reforms were carried out.
These included a move towards majority voting, instead of the unaninimity now required.
Toubon also urged greater powers for the European Commission to take initiatives in the justice field, and a stronger role for the European Court of Justice.
Other EU countries favoured moves to reconcile criminal and civil laws in a bid to close loopholes exploited by criminals.
The ideas remain controversial in Britain, which has singlehandedly blocked a number of justice issues in the past.

"We have to implement existing measures without trying for new ones," Britain's representative was quoted as telling the meeting, saying the EU had used its new justice powers well. Fog kept British Home Secretary Michael Howard away.

The EU's Justice Commissioner Anita Gradin told ministers that although 201 justice measures had been agreed since the Maastricht Treaty gave the bloc a limited justice role three years ago, there was no way of checking that they were being implemented.
And while EU members lament a lack of joint action to combat fraud and organised crime, conventions that could help solve the problems remained unratified.

A convention to bring into full operation the EU police agency Europol has been ratified only by Britain. Three other conventions, on fraud, customs cooperation and extradition, have not been ratified by any country.
